analysisMarkdown:
## Where gold sits in its 1-year context

Spot gold trades at **$3,562.39**, down 0.21% over the past 24 hours. That is a long way from the picture many investors still carry in their heads: the metal is **35.2% below its 52-week high of $5,496** set on 2026-01-29, and it is hovering just above its **52-week low of $3,533** printed on 2026-11-21. Price sits **10.2% below the 50-day average** ($3,966) and **15.4% below the 200-day average** ($4,211), and returns are negative across every window we track — **-12.6% over 20 days**, **-22.4% over 90 days**, and **-14.5% over 1 year**. In short, this is not record territory; it is a sustained downtrend with the market probing fresh 1-year lows.

The 20-day closing range runs from **$3,533 to $4,121**, and 20-day annualised volatility is about **30%**, so daily swings remain meaningful.

## The macro backdrop

The macro setting is firmly against gold right now. The Federal Reserve's trade-weighted **broad dollar index stands at 123.60**, up **2.26 over 30 days** and **5.54 over 90 days** — higher than **100% of readings in the past year**. A dollar near a 1-year high makes gold more expensive outside the US and is a direct headwind.

Real yields matter even more. The **10-year real yield is 2.79%**, up **0.13 pp over 30 days** and **0.45 pp over 90 days**, higher than **92% of the past year's readings**. Because gold pays no income, a rising real return on inflation-protected bonds raises the opportunity cost of holding it. The **10-year nominal Treasury yield is 4.91%**, while the **10-year inflation breakeven has eased to 2.12%** (down 0.22 pp over 30 days) — so the climb in real yields is being driven by rate expectations rather than higher inflation compensation.

## The scorecard in plain language

**Short term (1–4 weeks).** The scorecard reads **-5, a baseline SELL**. The heaviest weights are the **-12.6% 20-day return** (strongly adverse) and the **rising broad dollar** (strongly adverse), with price below its 50-day average and real yields higher over 30 days also counting against gold. The single supportive factor is contrarian: price is stretched **10.2% below** its 50-day average, which can eventually invite stabilisation. It is not enough to offset the rest.

**Long term (3–12 months).** The scorecard reads **-6, a baseline SELL**, with every component adverse: price below the 200-day average, the 50-day below the 200-day (a downtrend structure), the deeply negative 90-day return, the 35.2% distance from the 52-week high, and the 90-day increases in both real yields and the dollar. This is an unusually clean, one-directional reading.

## The events driving the market

The past few sessions delivered a cluster of data that pushed in the same direction. On 2026-11-25, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, **core PCE, came in hot (around 3.3% year over year, above forecasts)**, and the **second estimate of Q3 GDP was revised sharply higher to a 4.3% annual rate** from 3.4%. Strong growth plus sticky inflation is precisely the combination that keeps a central bank leaning toward tighter policy.

Markets responded by pricing a December rate increase as close to a done deal — implied odds moved to roughly **98%** for the 9 December decision, and some officials have floated the possibility of a larger move. Fed commentary in recent weeks has leaned toward tighter policy to tackle persistent inflation. Against that, gold **slid to a fresh 52-week low** as equity-market losses spilled into precious metals.

**Note on adjustments:** our rules only let us nudge a call for a dated, sourced event the scorecard cannot yet see. Every fresh event this week — inflation, growth, rate-hike pricing — points the **same, bearish** way, so there is no basis for a bullish step. The December 9 Fed meeting is a scheduled future event and cannot be used to adjust today. Both calls therefore stay at the default: **short-term SELL (medium confidence)** and **long-term SELL (high confidence)**.

## Outlook and risks

**Short-term outlook.** Conditions over the next 1–4 weeks look more challenging than supportive. Momentum is negative, the dollar is elevated and real yields are firm. The main two-way risk is the extreme stretch below trend: markets that fall this fast can snap back, and any genuine risk-off shock or dovish surprise could spark a sharp counter-move. This short-term view would be broken by a **daily close above $4,121**.

**Long-term outlook.** Over 3–12 months the trend, valuation-versus-averages and macro drivers all align to the downside. The risks to this bearish read are real but not yet in the data: a pivot in Fed expectations if growth or inflation cools, renewed geopolitical stress, or continued official-sector demand could change the complexion. Those are standing conditions or hypotheticals today, not dated events. This view would be broken by a **daily close above $4,673**.

For everyday investors, the takeaway is descriptive, not directive: the measurable setup currently favours caution over conviction, and the levels above are the lines that would signal the backdrop has genuinely shifted.
